title_en: Near in Spite of Distance, I Am Close to You
body_ar: قريبٌ على بُعدٍ أنا منكِ في الأسرى بدوية قفر بها جيف الحسرى .. يذكرني حالي وحالك قولةً بفارس حمدان الذي كابد الأسرى .. أيضحك مأسور وتبكي طليقة فصبرا فإن العسر يستصحب اليسرى .. وفيما مضى قد كنت تخشين ضرة .. فكانت بدار الشرطة الضرة العسرى .. نقيم بدار للهوان معدة فنلبس أوساخا ونفترش الغبرا .. ضفادعها في العد مثل بعوضها .. وداحسها في عدوه يسبق الغبرا .. ولكننا فيها أنسنا بربنـــا فنلنا سرورا لن تحيطوا به خبرا .. سعادتنا بالضيم في ذات ربنا .. تفوق بأضعافٍ سعادتنا الأخرى .. وأسورة فيها يصفد بعضنا .. تفوق التي قد كان يلبسها كسرى .. وإن لنا في الشعب والجب أسوة .. زنازننا إذ ذاك نحسبها قصرا .. يثور كتاب الله من كل غرفة .. إذا الليل أرخي من غدائره سترا .. وتسمع آناء النهار تلاوة .. فتسمع ترتيلا وتسمعها حدرا .. وتسمع في الأنحاء من كل سورةٍ .. وتسمعه سبعة وتسمعه عشرا .. نفوق آي الذكر في وجه من بغى .. فيبصرها الباغي الردينية السمرا .. ونصلتها بيضاً قواطع نورها .. يرد علي الباغي بواتره بترا .. فكم حجة لله فيها مبينة .. وكم شبهة للناس تدحرها دحرا .. بموعوده الآتي نجدد عزمنا .. ومن قصص الماضين نستلهم الصبرا .. مخازي بني صهيون نقرؤها به .. فنزداد بغضا للآلي دنسوا المسرى .. وإخوانهم من نافقوا كل أمرهم .. نراه عيانا واقعا بعد ما يقرا .. فإن سارعوا فيهم نسارع لــ جنة .. ومغفرة نرجوهما نحن في الأخرى .. وليس لهم ذاك الرجاء وإنما .. يؤخرهم ربي لبطشته الكبرى .. وما يبتغي الجهال منا فإننا .. أشداء لا بطشاً نخاف ولا غدرا .. أسود من آساد المهيمن تبتغي .. من الله في الأخرى المثوبة والأجرا .. بنهج قويم لا التطرف شأنه .. ولا اللين للتهديد والضغط والإغرا .. نسير على نهج النبي محمد .. ببيعة إيمان نرى نكثها كفرا .. ولله قد بعنا نفوسا أبية .. بربح عظيم فيه أربي لنا السعرا .. بأجسامنا نفدي وننصر ديننا .. وننشره نورا ونقبضـه جمرا .. ونمنعه حتى نصرع دونه .. وتنشر بالمنشار أجسامنا نشرا .. ولسنا نبالي خاذلينا فإنهم .. ضعاف وإنا دونهم نرتجي النصرا
body_en:
[Verse. Rendered as prose, line by line; the Arabic is the operative text.]

*Near in spite of distance, I am close to you — here among the captives, in a barren desert waste strewn with the carcasses of beasts broken by the road.*

*My condition and yours put me in mind of a line of the Knight of Hamdan, who endured captivity:*

*"Shall a captive laugh while a free woman weeps?" So be patient: hardship keeps ease in its company.*

*In time past you used to dread a co-wife — and the harsher co-wife turned out to be the police station.*

*We dwell in a house made ready for degradation: we wear filth for clothing and spread out the dust for a bed.*

*Its frogs are as many in number as its mosquitoes, and its Dahis, at the gallop, outstrips al-Ghabra.*

*And yet in it we found our intimacy with our Lord, and so attained a gladness of which you will never encompass any knowledge.*

*Our happiness under injustice, for our Lord's sake, surpasses many times over every other happiness of ours.*

*And the bracelets in which some of us are shackled surpass those that Chosroes used to wear.*

*We have a precedent in the mountain pass and in the well; our cells, reckoned so, we count as a palace.*

*The Book of God surges up from every room, when night lets down a veil from its tresses.*

*And through the hours of the day you hear recitation — you hear it measured (tartīl) and you hear it swift (ḥadr).*

*You hear, all about you, something of every sura; you hear it in the seven and you hear it in the ten.*

*We notch the verses of the Remembrance to the string in the face of the aggressor, and the aggressor sees them as tawny Rudayni spears.*

*We draw them as white, keen-edged blades whose light turns the aggressor's own cutting swords back upon him, cut for cut.*

*How many a clear proof of God is in them, and how many a doubt raised among people they drive utterly off.*

*By His promise that is yet to come we renew our resolve, and from the stories of those who went before we draw our patience.*

*In it we read the disgraces of the sons of Zion, and so we grow in hatred for those who defiled the place of the Night Journey,*

*and their brethren, those who play the hypocrite: we see the whole of their affair before our eyes, coming to pass just as it is read.*

*If they hasten towards them, we hasten towards a garden and a forgiveness — for which we hope in the hereafter.*

*They have no such hope; my Lord only defers them for His greater onslaught.*

*And whatever the ignorant may want of us — we are firm: we fear neither violence nor treachery,*

*lions from among the lions of the Overseer (al-Muhaymin), seeking from God in the hereafter reward and recompense,*

*on a straight course whose way is neither extremism nor pliancy before threat, pressure and inducement.*

*We walk the way of the Prophet Muhammad, under a pledge of faith the breaking of which we hold to be unbelief.*

*To God we have sold souls that will not be brought low, at a great profit, in which He has multiplied the price for us.*

*With our bodies we pay the ransom and we give our religion its victory; we spread it abroad as light and grasp it as live coal.*

*And we defend it until we are struck down in its defence, and our bodies are sawn asunder with the saw.*

*We pay no heed to those who forsake us: they are weak, and we, without them, look for victory.*

flags.arabic: مخازي بني صهيون نقرؤها به .. فنزداد بغضا للآلي دنسوا المسرى
flags.context: the poem’s two most politically charged lines, read together with وإخوانهم من نافقوا and مع اليهود مطبعين in the companion poem at 1113
options: the disgraces of the sons of Zion
the disgraces of the followers of Zion
flags.note: EDITORIAL. بنو صهيون is literally "the sons of Zion" and is idiomatically directed at the Zionist movement and the Israeli state rather than at Jews as such, but the phrase does not itself draw that line, and the poem speaks of growing in بغض (hatred) towards those it names. Translated faithfully, neither softened nor strengthened. Published in English without context, this line carries reputational risk and, in some European jurisdictions, potential legal exposure under incitement-to-hatred provisions. The decision whether and how to publish belongs to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh’s office (style guide section 12).

flags.arabic: بأجسامنا نفدي ... ونمنعه حتى نصرع دونه .. وتنشر بالمنشار أجسامنا نشرا
flags.context: the closing movement of the poem, immediately after بنهج قويم لا التطرف شأنه
options: martyrdom imagery in the classical register: readiness to be killed rather than to kill
figurative language for steadfastness under interrogation
flags.note: EDITORIAL. The imagery is of enduring death, not of inflicting it — it draws on the hadith of the believer sawn in two — and the poem expressly disavows extremism two lines earlier (بنهج قويم لا التطرف شأنه). Read in English out of that context, however, the passage can be taken for something it is not. Flagged for a conscious publication decision rather than for any change to the translation.

flags.context: describing the vermin of the prison cell
options: its Dahis, at the gallop, outstrips al-Ghabra (the two legendary racehorses whose race began the War of Dahis and al-Ghabra)
its swiftest vermin outrun the rest
wordplay on الغبراء as both the mare’s name and the dust of the floor
flags.note: A mock-heroic allusion: the cell’s insects are cast as the two famous racehorses of pre-Islamic legend. The pun on الغبرا (al-Ghabra the mare / the dust just mentioned in the previous line) cannot be carried into English. Option 0 keeps the allusion and loses the pun; a reviewer may prefer a footnote.

flags.context: describing Qur’an recitation heard through the prison
options: you hear it in the seven readings and in the ten (the canonical qirāʼāt)
you hear it seven times over and ten times over
you hear seven reciters of it and ten
flags.note: The preceding line names the recitation tempos tartīl and ḥadr, which is technical tajwīd vocabulary and makes the canonical seven and ten readings the natural sense. The numerals are bare, however, and a simple "seven times, ten times" is grammatically available. Not resolved.

translator_notes: A poem, not a fatwa. The schema has no verse type, so type is set to "article"; the record should be displayed as poetry, not as a ruling. Nothing in it states a legal ruling and none has been inferred.
Rendered as prose line by line, per style guide section 4; no rhymed English has been attempted, and the Arabic is retained as the operative text.
The poem was written in detention. It is addressed to a woman — the second person is feminine singular throughout — most naturally the poet’s wife.

Line 3 quotes the celebrated line of Abu Firas al-Hamdani from his Byzantine captivity, "Shall a captive laugh while a free man weeps?", with طليق altered to the feminine طليقة to fit the addressee. The quotation marks in the English mark it as a quotation; the Arabic does not mark it.

أربى في السعر (line 26) is the ordinary lexical sense of the root, "to increase, to multiply", and carries no reference to ribā as a legal category. It has deliberately not been rendered with any usury vocabulary.

Several phrases echo the Qur’an without being marked as quotation in the source: لن تحيطوا به خبرا (cf. Sūrat al-Kahf 18:68), سارعوا (cf. Sūrat Āl ʻImrān 3:133 and Sūrat al-Māʼidah 5:52), and لبطشته الكبرى (cf. Sūrat al-Dukhān 44:16). They are translated as the poet’s own words, with the echoes noted here rather than converted into citations.

The source contains typographic artefacts from the CMS: tatweel elongation characters inside words (بربنـــا, ونقبضـه) and a stray elongation with a space in لــ جنة for لجنة. These are preserved verbatim in body_ar and are not reproduced in body_en. This is a corpus-wide cleanup matter, not a per-record fix (style guide section 11).

Line 28 alludes to the hadith of the believers before us whose bodies were sawn in two, and line 27 to the hadith of holding to one’s religion as one grasps a live coal. Neither is cited in the Arabic, so neither has been supplied with an attribution or a grading.
dec: A poem that speaks of growing in hatred toward those it names. Potential exposure under incitement-to-hatred provisions in several European states.
